name: Shohei Ohtani
season_outlook: Ohtani has scripted quite the résumé already over his seven MLB seasons: Rookie of the Year (2018), MVP honors (2021), first player in history to hit 30-plus homers while also striking out 200-plus batters (2022), back-to-back MVPs (2023-24) and, most recently, becoming the charter member of baseball's 50/50 club (2024). While further history book rewrites might seem logically unattainable for the now-30-year-old, it's still within the realm of possibility that he'll score a career-high total fantasy points in 2025 and/or set a personal best in Wins Above Replacement. As both a hitter and pitcher from 2021-23 -- his expected role once again in 2025 -- Ohtani averaged 214 fantasy points more than the league's next-best player annually, an advantage that can be readily exploited in ESPN's standard game with its daily transaction format. Ohtani's fantasy utility hinges heavily upon how your league handles him, but a universal, No. 1 overall case is a relatively easy one.

name: Logan Webb
season_outlook: Webb continues to be one of the game's most durable and reliable starters, despite fanning hitters at a below-average clip. Control and command remain Webb's bread and butter, along with an extreme groundball rate. His 613 innings since 2022 lead the majors, but his 529 strikeouts over that span rank 15th. Webb's ERA and WHIP are both top 10 among all starters with at least 500 innings over the past three seasons, but both are vulnerable to variance since Webb allows so many balls in play. Feeding into the concern is the fact that Webb's swinging-strike rate has declined each of the past three seasons. Accepting the low strikeout discount on Webb has been a fruitful endeavor, but it's reached the point where doing so invites more risk than may be evident by recent performance.

name: Tarik Skubal
season_outlook: Coming off a sizzling finish to 2023 where he scored the most SP fantasy points across his final eight starts, Skubal exploded with a 2024 for the ages, culminating in the AL Cy Young Award. He maintained his 2023 control gains (sixth-ranked 4.6 BB%), added another full tick to his average fastball velocity (third-ranked 96.8 mph), and delivered 20-plus fantasy points in a MLB-leading (tied with Zack Wheeler) 14 of his 31 starts. Best yet, Skubal maintained elite performance across the entire six-month calendar, scoring more points over the Tigers' final 81 regular-season games (279) than in their first 81 (274). It placed him at the forefront of the fantasy SP rankings, though as is true with almost any pitcher these days, he's not completely without risk, with 2017 Tommy John and August 2022 flexor tendon surgeries on his résumé. Hey, sometimes you have to close your eyes tight and roll the dice.

name: Freddy Peralta
season_outlook: Tasked with taking over the No. 1 starter role for Milwaukee following Corbin Burnes' departure via trade, Peralta performed admirably in 2024, albeit not quite to the level of his ace predecessor. His strikeout and walk rates went in the wrong direction and he had some issues with the long ball, particularly at home, allowing 1.72 HR/9 at American Family Field. Peralta also had trouble the third time through the order, posting a 7.52 ERA, a far cry from the 3.86 mark he posted the third time through in 2023. Nonetheless, he reached double-digit wins for the third time in four seasons as the Brewers ran away with the NL Central. While he may be miscast as an ace, Peralta has reached 30 starts and 200 strikeouts in back-to-back seasons. He totaled a career-high 173.2 innings last year and will be a bargain for the team at an $8 million price tag for 2025.

name: Cristopher Sanchez
season_outlook: Sanchez impressed by going 11-9 with a 3.32 ERA and 1.24 WHIP across 181.2 innings last season, his first as a full-time member of the Philadelphia rotation. The lefty's game is built around the sinking fastball which was the main driver in a 57.4 percent groundball rate last season, third highest among qualified starters. In turn, he allowed just 11 homers for the third-best HR/9 among that group. Sanchez can also pull the string on a changeup and spin a breaking ball, though the package has not included many strikeouts to date. It's possible that Sanchez, still just 28 years old, could unlock another level with the strikeouts, but that should not be expected since there is little reason to mess with a formula that has been largely successful. The K rate as it stands now caps his upside, but Sanchez looks like a viable pick to fill out any fantasy rotation in 2025.

name: Paul Skenes
season_outlook: It has been a whirlwind past two years for Skenes. His LSU Tigers won the 2023 College World Series behind his performance that earned him its Most Outstanding Player Award and he won the Dick Howser Trophy as college baseball's best player. Skenes was then selected No. 1 overall in that July's amateur draft, ultimately reaching the majors with the Pirates just 10 months later. He'd toss six hitless, 11-strikeout frames in only his second start, kicking off a historic campaign that ultimately earned him NL Rookie of the Year honors. Skenes' electric raw stuff (a 99-mph average fastball, slider and splinker) grades among the best in the majors already despite his youth, and he's already drawing favorite's odds for the 2025 Cy Young Award -- a testament to his overwhelming upside. If there's any reason to hesitate in building your fantasy team around him, it's that the Pirates have been cautious with his workload, coupled with the typical worries we have with young pitchers throwing large IP totals. But hey, isn't every pitcher an injury risk to some degree?

name: Garrett Crochet
season_outlook: Crochet didn't merely break out in his first season back in a pitching rotation since his Tennessee days -- his 2024 performance was historic. He became the first pitcher in the modern era to strike out at least 140 batters with 20 walks or fewer through his first 18 career starts, and seven consecutive strikeouts to begin his Sept. 1 start tied an AL record. Despite the White Sox's concerns about his workload, which increased over the course of the summer, Crochet maintained elite underlying skills, even if his 5.12 second-half ERA belied his talent. The Red Sox acquired him with the hopes he can further blossom into their staff ace. Considering his arrow pointed nowhere but up for the entirety of 2024, there's reason to believe he will. Crochet is a building-block pitcher for fantasy purposes.

name: Edwin Diaz
season_outlook: Diaz's first season back following right patellar tendon surgery looked shaky on its surface, but his underlying skills nevertheless had the look of a top-shelf closer. A trio of hideous early-season outings bloated his ERA, and a shoulder impingement cost him a few weeks shortly thereafter, but across the season's final three-plus months he had 15 saves (with a 2.41 ERA) and he tied for 11th in RP fantasy points. A winter of rest could do a world of good for Diaz, granting him a full ramping-up process and typical spring training. He'll return as the Mets' closer, a role from which he has twice struck out 90-plus hitters and twice saved 30-plus games (and don't forget he also had one season of each with the Mariners). He should be drafted among the first at his position in fantasy leagues.

name: Andres Munoz
season_outlook: Munoz enters the 2025 season in a slightly different situation from just one year ago. He was not the clearcut favorite for the primary closer role last spring after the acquisition of Gregory Santos from the White Sox as well as the impressive work from Matt Brash in 2023. Yet, Munoz was the last man standing and he is now the clear frontrunner for saves in Seattle. He managed to avoid the injured list last season despite dealing with some back issues, earning an appearance in the All-Star Game. Munoz has twice now posted ERAs below 2.50 and WHIPs below 1.00 in the past three seasons, and the outstanding Seattle rotation and suspect offense almost ensure that there will be many late and close opportunities for Munoz to finally get to 30 saves in 2025.

name: Chris Sale
season_outlook: Sale's Comeback Player of the Year campaign earned him his first career Cy Young Award in 2024, fueled by what were his best single-year strikeout, whiff and hard-hit rates allowed as well as his best average fastball velocity since before his March 2020 Tommy John surgery. Best yet, he only seemed to improve as the season progressed, posting a 1.88 ERA and a 33.2% strikeout rate across his final 16 starts, signaling his ability to maintain an elite level of performance despite his 35 years of age. Back issues prematurely ended Sale's campaign. That's an injury which bears watching throughout spring training, but if he's in the clear on that front, he's plenty capable of delivering top-10 fantasy SP numbers again.

name: Logan Gilbert
season_outlook: Amidst a bevy of talented, fastball-throwing frontline starters in Seattle, Gilbert has quietly emerged as a prospective ace. He has made noticeable gains in numerous statistical categories over the past two seasons, including WHIP, walk, strikeout, whiff and ground ball rates. Plus, he has cut roughly a half a run from his Statcast expected ERA in both of those campaigns. Gilbert's addition of a splitter in 2023 helped him become a more strikeout-oriented starter, and his move to a six-pitch repertoire with less fastball reliance in 2024 helped further diversify his skill set. While the Mariners offense probably hasn't improved to the point that he'll significantly boost last year's nine wins, Gilbert should again deliver excellent numbers otherwise. He's a solid fantasy building block.

name: Robert Suarez
season_outlook: Suarez delivered in his first season as the Padres' regular closer, converting 36 of 42 save chances. It's slightly concerning that half of Suarez's blown saves came in September, a month during which he posted a 6.00 ERA and 1.50 WHIP. However, he shook it off and logged three saves in the final week of the season and then two more in the playoffs. Suarez's strikeout rate isn't dominant, especially for a closer, but last season his 6.2 percent walk rate was the fourth lowest among relievers with at least 20 saves. Suarez is the favorite for saves in San Diego, but last year was his first fully healthy season and he'll be 34 years old in 2025, so rostering setup man Jason Adam in tandem with Suarez may be a wise move.

name: Kevin Gausman
season_outlook: Gausman wasn't quite himself last year after a bout of shoulder fatigue in spring training interrupted his preparations for the start of the season. The right-hander's velocity was down a tick in 2024 -- several ticks early on -- and the strikeouts dipped along with it. His surface numbers improved over the final two months, but the strikeouts never really rebounded, as he was below a 20 percent K rate in both August and September. Just one year ago, Gausman was treated as a borderline ace following a late-career breakout built on the strength of his trademark splitter. The market has perhaps overcorrected heading into 2025, though the massive decline in whiffs and tough division leave performance question marks and provide reason to invest elsewhere. Now 34, Gausman has two years remaining on his deal with the Blue Jays.

name: Yoshinobu Yamamoto
season_outlook: Yamamoto, one of the most ballyhooed Japanese arrivals of the past decade-plus, had a U.S. debut season that will be regarded by most as a disappointment. From the five runs in just a single inning's work he surrendered in his big-league debut last March, to the near-three months he missed due to a triceps injury, he never got much of an extended chance to showcase his tremendous raw stuff. Yamamoto did, however, enjoy a 12-start stretch with a 2.41 ERA and 28.5% strikeout rate, and his four-seam fastball, splitter and curveball each registered excellent marks. The ingredients of a staff ace -- granted one subject to the six-man rotation and a probable innings cap -- are still here.

name: Max Fried
season_outlook: Fried finds himself pitching for a new organization after spending the last nine seasons in the Atlanta organization, as the Yankees gave Fried a sizable deal despite the time missed in 2023 with a forearm strain as well as the neuritis in his pitching elbow in the middle of the 2024 season. The left-hander's ability to limit homers will be tested at Yankee Stadium, but left-center field being forgiving to his particular approach -- at least on paper -- should help balance things out in his favor. Fried throws seven different pitch types to both righties and lefties which puts hitters into uncomfortable situations. His ability to keep hitters off balance is why he is elite at limiting hard contact and why his ERA has just once been above 3.25 in a full season of work. The only risk associated with Fried would be a recurrence of the forearm issue from 2023 as the skills are more than steady.

name: Mason Miller
season_outlook: Miller's campaign was one of the most underappreciated -- not only in 2024, but across all historical rookie RP seasons. He became only the third rookie reliever to manage at least 25 saves, 100 strikeouts and a sub-2.50 ERA (Terry Forster, 1972; Craig Kimbrel, 2011), and among all pitchers with at least 50 IP in 2024, he led in strikeout rate (41.8%), average fastball velocity (100.9 mph) and Statcast-expected ERA (1.77). Miller, who previously had durability concerns, missed only two weeks' time to injury when he fractured his pinky punching a padded table, and a short-relief role seemed to suit his skill set. He has assumed a place as one of the game's best fantasy relievers, and it's a plus for 2025 that his Athletics made winter moves hinting at more of a push to compete.

name: Joe Ryan
season_outlook: While Ryan has established himself as a quality starting pitcher in Major League Baseball, injuries have delayed the full-on breakout. He went down in August with a Grade 2 teres major strain and never made it back onto the field last season, though the Twins said in November that Ryan was making good progress in his recovery. A groin injury derailed his 2023 season, but through it all the right-hander has made 79 starts over the past three seasons (31st in the majors in that span). His flyball tendencies make him susceptible to homers, but Ryan is stingy with walks and misses bats at an above-average clip with his five-pitch mix. More cautious players will want to wait and see how Ryan looks in the spring before jumping in with both feet while those with a higher level of risk tolerance should be eager to invest in the skills.

name: Hunter Brown
season_outlook: Who'd have thought that the same Astros pitcher who surrendered nine runs without escaping the first inning of an April 2024 start would go on to score the 10th-most fantasy points among pitchers across the season's final five months? The introduction of a sinker in May played a big part in that, giving Brown a pitch to minimize hard contact to go along with his 96-mph fastball and whiff-generating knuckle curve. With his more balanced repertoire, he's now capable of top-25 fantasy SP numbers on the high end of his valuation curve. Brown is well worth a mid-round selection in all formats.

name: Carlos Rodon
season_outlook: Rodon got off to a fantastic start in 2024, going 9-2 with a 2.92 ERA and 1.05 WHIP across his first 80 innings (14 starts). He hit some bumps in the road during the summer months, and his season ended on a sour note with three home runs allowed over 3.1 innings in his lone World Series appearance against the Dodgers. Regardless, his 2024 campaign goes down as a considerable success after back, forearm and hamstring injuries cost him half of the previous year and sapped his effectiveness in his first season with the Yankees. His innings totals and performance have been all over the map throughout his career and he's now 32 years old, but recent history bodes rather favorably since Rodon has provided quality numbers across 30-plus starts in two of the past three years. He tentatively lines up as the Yankees' No. 3 starter entering 2025.

name: Jhoan Duran
season_outlook: Duran is coming off a second consecutive 20-plus-save season, though his role in the Minnesota bullpen has been somewhat in fluid, more so than fantasy managers would like. As a rookie in 2022, he blew batters away with an 18.1 percent swinging-strike rate and an elite strikeout-minus-walk percentage. However, he has not been able to achieve the same level of overall success over the past two seasons. This past year saw a reduction in his strikeout rate while opponents hit 28 points higher against Duran. He also struggled to prevent runners from scoring when they got on base. It feels like a pitcher with this much swing and miss and such a high groundball rate should have better outcomes than what Duran has earned to date. The expected stats show what Duran's is capable of.

name: Hunter Greene
season_outlook: Greene was in the midst of a breakthrough 2024, posting nine wins, 13 quality starts, a 2.83 ERA, a 1.02 WHIP and 162 strikeouts through his first 24 starts, before right elbow soreness derailed the rest of his season. He did return in time to make two solid appearances in late September, but the absence added to what has been an alarming injury history in his young MLB career, including IL stints at least five weeks in length in each of his three seasons. Greene has long possessed front-of-the-rotation stuff and, with better luck in the health department, he might yet realize that status in 2025. He's a prospective top-30 fantasy starter with upside, well worth a pick in the middle rounds of your draft.

name: Framber Valdez
season_outlook: Elbow inflammation put Valdez on the shelf early on last year, but he made a quick recovery and ended up totaling 176.1 innings during the 2024 regular season, pitching to a stellar 2.91 ERA and 1.11 WHIP. The left-hander has never been the most dominant arm in terms of strikeouts, but he generates groundballs at an incredibly high clip -- over 60 percent for his career -- mostly on the strength of his sinking fastball. High whiff rates on his secondaries suggest there may be some untapped strikeout potential, though Valdez is already 31 years old and paying for another level would be ill advised. Valdez leads the majors in wins with 44 over the past three seasons and will be in position to reach double digits for the Astros once again before potentially hitting free agency next winter.

name: Jacob deGrom
season_outlook: DeGrom has managed to put up just 197.1 innings over the past four seasons due to his body constantly failing him, which is a shame considering he's one of the best pitchers of this generation. The right-hander last worked a full season in 2019 when he pitched his third consecutive season of 200-plus innings while winning his second consecutive Cy Young Award. He made it back for three starts at the end of 2024 and essentially picked up where he left off with 14 strikeouts and one walk over those outings. This remains the ultimate risk/reward pick because at least Tyler Glasnow is good for 100-plus innings in a season around his injuries while deGrom has barely worked 100 innings over the previous three seasons combined. Even 100 innings of deGrom brilliance would be more valuable to a roster than 150 innings of another arm, but expecting that sort of workload might be optimistic.

name: Luis Castillo
season_outlook: Castillo's season ended in early September as a result of a hamstring strain, but he's expected to be 100 percent in the spring. Previously more of an groundball pitcher in Great American Ball Park, he has adjusted to T-Mobile Park, inducing more flyballs. Even in the bigger yard, Castillo's homers have increased, though the corresponding drop in BABIP has lowered his WHIP, so he is no longer a detriment in that category. After two seasons with a strikeout rate over 27 percent, Castillo slid to 24.3 percent last season, coinciding with a drop in swinging-strike rate. His once vaunted changeup lost some of its effectiveness, likely due to his four-seam fastball dropping a couple of ticks. He was once a borderline fantasy ace, but Castillo is now merely solid as he enters his age-32 season.

name: Aroldis Chapman
season_outlook: Chapman has not saved 15 games in a season since 2021, largely because of his propensity for walking batters, which is is too problematic for full-time closing duties. Yes, Chapman strikes out a high volume of hitters to offset his walks, but his walk rate has been at or above 15 percent each of the past four seasons. Walking a tight-rope in Pittsburgh is one thing; doing it in Fenway for half the season as well the other parks of the AL East is another. Boston also has other options such as Justin Slaten and the recovering Liam Hendriks for the ninth inning. Chapman's fastball velocity is still among the best in the league and homers are not as frequent as one might think. If Chapman could somehow get his walk rate back to a single-digit mark, he could once again be a high-end closer. However, that seems unlikely at 37 years old considering the fact Chapman has but once had a single-digit walk rate over the last eight seasons.

name: Nick Pivetta
season_outlook: Pivetta has had his moments of fantasy greatness over the years, best exemplified on a cumulative basis by his having the 13th-most strikeouts across the past four seasons. Still, his hot spells have unfortunately been too few and too far between. Injuries, occasional wildness and an extreme fly-ball rate have been the obstacles standing in his path towards something more, though he did finish 2024 with a 3.92 ERA and a 29.7% strikeout rate across his final 14 starts. That gives some hope for a step forward. Pivetta did linger on the free-agent market deep into the winter, but so long as he lands a committed rotation spot somewhere, he'll be worth a mid-round pick with greater appeal in points league scoring.

name: Sonny Gray
season_outlook: The Cardinals signed Gray to a three-year contract in November of 2023, but GM John Mozeliak made it clear this winter that lowering payroll is a priority heading into the 2025 season. With that, Gray is on the block, though he has a full no-trade clause. He won 13 games last season, his most since 2015, and finished third among qualified starters in strikeout percentage. Gray ended the season in the injured list with right forearm flexor tendonitis, but he was expected to have a normal offseason. Whether he stays in St. Louis or goes is a matter of little concern, since Gray is used to bouncing around the league. Health remains his biggest obstacle. The 35-year-old has averaged just over 150 innings per year over the past four seasons.

name: Shota Imanaga
season_outlook: Imanaga got off to a historic start with the Cubs last season, posting a 0.84 ERA across his first 53.2 innings, the lowest mark ever through a pitcher's first nine MLB starts. The lefty earned an All-Star selection in his first season stateside and finished third in the National League with 15 wins, while only George Kirby and Tarik Skubal ranked higher among qualified starters in terms of strikeout-to-walk ratio. Home runs were a problem on occasion -- Imanaga allowed multiple homers seven times -- and those concerns will follow him into 2025, as fantasy managers may hold their breath in tough matchups. The Cubs are working with him on that issue, and overall his stuff translated quite well as he made the jump from Nippon Professional Baseball at 30 years old. Expect some giveback, but Imanaga looks like a legitimate frontline starter, one probably best viewed as an SP2 for fantasy purposes.

name: Cole Ragans
season_outlook: Ragans' follow-up to his astonishing, late-2023 breakthrough went about as well as could possibly have been expected. He maintained almost every statistical gain across his by-far professional bests of 32 starts and 186 1/3 IP, with the only knock on his skills being his losing a tick on his average fastball velocity. Throwing 95.4 mph, however, makes him no slouch in terms of raw stuff, and pitching half of his games in one of the most pitcher-friendly environments helps bolster his case to be a true staff ace. Ragans should be drafted among the top 10 at his position, regardless of format.

name: Dylan Cease
season_outlook: Cease rebounded from a disappointing 2023 with a 2024 that, by many measures, was every bit as meaningful as his breakthrough 2022. Though his ERA (3.47) paled in comparison to 2022 (2.20), he set personal bests with his 8.5% walk rate and 1.07 WHIP. He recaptured the near-entirety of his lost fastball velocity, elevated his ground-ball rate to its highest number since his 2019 debut year, and averaged a near-identical number of innings per start (5.7). Best yet, Cease finished the year on a high note, posting a 2.58 ERA across his final 15 starts. He's also one of the game's most durable starters, having made at least 32 starts in each of the past four years. Cease is a bona fide fantasy staff ace and one well worth a pick in the opening rounds.

name: Tyler Glasnow
season_outlook: Glasnow's season was cut short in August by a right elbow injury, one first labeled as tendonitis but later diagnosed as a sprain following a failed attempt at a return. He said in an offseason interview that imaging in late October appeared to show the elbow being fully healed. While he set a new career high in innings last season before going down, that number being just 134 tells the story. Glasnow had Tommy John surgery in 2021 after missing time earlier in his career with shoulder and forearm trouble, flashing consistent brilliance in between. He had been trending in the right direction with his workload since TJS and proved to be a nice fit in Los Angeles, but his latest injury makes expectations tough to pin down entering 2025. Even if the talented 6-foot-8 righty is healthy and cruising, the Dodgers will probably need to limit him at some point given his injury history.

name: Jeff Hoffman
season_outlook: Hoffman broke through in a big way in 2023 while pitching in middle relief for the Phillies. Last season, he upped the ante even further by slashing another 3% off his walk rate. Between that and his sharing of the closer duties with Jose Alvarado, Carlos Estevez and Matt Strahm, Hoffman managed a top-20 season, both in rotisserie and points-based scoring. Now with the Blue Jays, Hoffman should take over full-time closer duties, a role from which he could take yet another step forward into the upper tier at his position. Draft him accordingly.

name: Blake Snell
season_outlook: Oh, what his 2024 season might have been had he come to contract terms before March 19. Snell struggled to get up to speed across the season's first three months, spending time on the IL due to adductor and groin issues, but once he found his groove, he managed a 1.23 ERA, a 38.1% strikeout rate and the majors' most fantasy points across his final 14 starts. Snell does have a history of statistical peaks over seasonal portions rather than the whole, but he also possesses multiple Cy Young Awards (2018, 2023), and his second-best-in-baseball 2.82 ERA (minimum 300 innings) across the past three seasons points to him likely being at an overall high point. The Dodgers should do well managing his workload and getting the most out of him, and there's a very real chance that Snell will rebound to rank among his position's best performers.

name: Bryan Woo
season_outlook: Considering the number of injuries that dogged him -- elbow trouble that cost him the first six weeks, forearm discomfort that cost him a June start, and a hamstring strain that sidelined him for 2 1/2 weeks in July -- Woo's 2024, which earned him a top-30 SP valuation in roto formats, was rather surprising. He has some of the best control in baseball, his 2.8% walk rate was best in baseball among those with at least 100 IP, and he had a 2.95 ERA over his last 29 big-league starts. Still, Woo's elbow and forearm issues raise future concerns about his durability. Monitor him carefully during spring training, but with better injury luck, he should deliver top-50 fantasy SP value.

name: Raisel Iglesias
season_outlook: Iglesias and Atlanta has been a match made in heaven, as he's posted a 1.96 ERA and 0.92 WHIP in 151.1 innings spanning 152 appearances over the past two and a half seasons. He shaved his WHIP to just 0.74 last season and reached the 30-save threshold for the fifth time in his career. Iglesias lost a little bit off his strikeout rate and benefited from a .199 BABIP, but that's picking nits. All four of his pitches had BAAs under .180 and he went without allowing an earned run for about half the season from mid-June to mid-September. Now 35 years old, Iglesias will be pitching for a big payday next winter in the final year of his deal. There's always a chance he could be dealt if Atlanta falls out of contention, but the right-hander enters the year with a ton of job security in his current situation.

name: Michael King
season_outlook: The centerpiece of the 2023-24 offseason's Juan Soto trade, King proved every bit as capable a starting pitcher across 30 starts for the Padres last season as he was over an eight-start stint for the Yankees to conclude 2023. In fact, King was one of only four pitchers to strike out at least 200 batters with a sub-3.00 ERA, joining both Cy Young Award winners (Chris Sale, Tarik Skubal) and Zack Wheeler. He only strengthened his underlying numbers over the season's second half, getting a whiff nearly one-third of the time hitters swung at any of his pitches. It sets up the right-hander well for a similarly productive 2025, albeit with some risk of ERA regression, as his Statcast xERA should be nearly three-quarters of a run higher. Still, that's a top-20 capable fantasy starter regardless of format.

name: George Kirby
season_outlook: Few pitchers have ever possessed the kind of control that Kirby has shown. His 3.1% walk rate, through three MLB seasons, is already the lowest among pitchers with at least as many starts as he has during the modern era. But don't conflate that for a pitcher who peppers the strike zone with so-so stuff. Kirby's 96.0 mph fastball, slider, sinker, splitter and knuckle curve gives him a sound, consistently elite repertoire that should make him an annual candidate for top-10 fantasy SP seasons. In order to take the next step and perhaps score big Cy Young votes, he'd probably need to reintroduce his whiff-generating splitter of 2023, but even without it he's the kind of pitcher around whom you'll want to build.

name: Josh Hader
season_outlook: Consistency is tough to find in the late innings. Even the greats like Hader endure some statistical variance -- he had a 5.22 ERA in a difficult 2022 season -- and it comes with the territory of facing the best hitters in the world in the highest-leverage spots night after night. Hader tallied 34 saves in his first year with Houston and has now racked up 30-plus saves in each of the last five full MLB seasons. The left-hander occasionally toes the line with walks and home runs, but his sinking fastball and swing-and-miss slider form a highly effective 1-2 punch. While the Astros have done some retooling this winter, but there is little reason to think Hader won't be the closer for Houston in 2025, with the flexibility and dominance to exceed 100 strikeouts in relief.

name: Spencer Strider
season_outlook: The 2024 season was a disaster for Strider and his fantasy managers, as the No. 1 pitcher off most draft boards lasted just two starts before succumbing to season-ending elbow surgery -- though he had an internal brace procedure this time after having Tommy John surgery previously in 2019. That gives the right-hander hope of returning in the early stages of 2025. Stiil, there is always risk of setbacks or diminished performance in pitchers initially returning from such a significant operation. When healthy, Strider has been the game's best strikeout artist -- his 458 K's across his span of 54 healthy starts from May 2022-April 2024 were 51 more than the next-closest hurler -- so he'll naturally slide in as one of this year's top risk/reward pitcher picks. Monitor his rehabilitation throughout spring training, as his prognosis could drive his draft value as high as a top-25 SP pick or more of a late-round flier.

name: Ranger Suarez
season_outlook: Suarez began the 2024 season by going 9-0 with a minuscule 1.36 ERA and 0.79 WHIP across his first 66 innings, only to slide to 3-8 with a 5.10 ERA and 1.52 WHIP over his subsequent 17 starts. The left-hander was said to be dealing with back tightness around the All-Star break and he eventually landed on the injured list as a result of the injury. Despite the way his season trended, it still has to be considered a highly successful campaign, one that further established Suarez as a quality mid-rotation starter in MLB. He is not the most dominant arm in terms of strikeouts, but Suarez keeps the ball on the ground and has one of the National League's best offenses to power him to wins. It's also not crazy to hold out hope that Suarez may still be able to add to his workload in his age-29 season after making the transition from the bullpen a few years ago.

name: Zac Gallen
season_outlook: No longer is Gallen being drafted as a borderline ace. He missed roughly a month of the 2024 season with a hamstring injury and his walk rate increased by more than three percentage points, which led to his WHIP jumping from 1.12 to 1.26. Gallen's knuckle curve remains an excellent put-away pitch, but his four-seam fastball and slider were entirely hittable last season. Perhaps Gallen has fallen further than he should. After all, the right-hander was a Cy Young finalist in the National League in 2023, he won 14 games in a down year and still does a lot well relative to most starting pitchers in MLB, including limiting homers. Take the name away and the underlying profile is not all that exciting, but Gallen's numbers over the last three years give him a case to be viewed as a third or fourth starter in fantasy entering 2025.

name: Carlos Estevez
season_outlook: Signed by the Royals at the end of January, Estevez figures to battle Lucas Erceg, primarily, for saves to begin 2025, and his eight-digit salary probably gives him a leg up in that competition. Estevez managed a career-best 27.8% strikeout rate in his first full season as a closer in 2023, then added enough gains in terms of control last year to serve as a competent, well above-average closer. Fantasy managers will want to monitor the Royals' bullpen pecking order through the Cactus League schedule -- saves carry a three-point advantage over holds in ESPN standard leagues -- but regardless of role, Estevez is a reliever well worth taking in the late rounds.

name: Robbie Ray
season_outlook: Ray's rehab from May 2023 Tommy John surgery extended into late July, and from there, he managed to make just seven starts before being shut down in late August with a strained hamstring. Ray threw 30.2 innings with 43 punchouts and 15 walks, along with six homers. His velocity returned to 2021 levels and his path looks typical for a pitcher recovering from TJS -- the strikeouts come back first, and then command and control. Ray struggles with home runs, making it all the more important that he limit the free passes. His home venue is ideal for streaming, but it may be best to wait and gauge his health and command in the spring before investing.

name: Tanner Bibee
season_outlook: Even though Bibee's ERA in 2024 was half a run higher than his rookie season, he improved his strikeout and walk rates to the point his 20.1% K-BB% mark was the 13th best among qualified pitchers. His home run rate ticked up, but it was still below the league average. Bibee's four-seam fastball registered a -8.5 pitch value after landing at 6.5 in his rookie season. However, he generated more swinging strikes and threw it in the zone more often last season. Last year's Hard-Hit and Barrel Rates against were lower than his rookie season, but the BABIP on his four-seamer was higher, driving down the pitch value. Consider the oddity as something to monitor but not detract from his status as one of the top young starters in the game.

name: Brandon Pfaadt
season_outlook: The breakthrough didn't appear to happen for Pfaadt during his first full MLB season and, if you consider surface numbers only, his 6.60 ERA across his final 12 starts was unsightly. A check beneath the hood, however, reveals signs of growth that might ultimately lead to a front-of-a-fantasy-rotation role as early as 2025. Thanks to increased sinker usage, he added 10% to his ground-ball rate, and he boosted his strikeout rate during the season's second half, exemplified by his registering three double-digit strikeout performances over his final nine starts. Pfaadt, whom scouts regarded highly at the time of his MLB debut, is one of the better profit-potential starters you'll find in the middle rounds of mixed leagues.

name: Andrew Abbott
season_outlook: Abbott was limited to 25 starts after his season ended in mid-August due to a strained shoulder, but he's expected to be healthy for spring training. His 3.72 ERA is misleading as shown by a less impressive 4.91 xFIP and 4.78 SIERA. A high 82.9% left on base mark rescued his season. Abbott's strikeout rate plummeted to 19.5%, down from 26.1% in his rookie season. His velocity and repertoire didn't change, so perhaps Abbott needs to be less predictable with his sequencing. He's slated to be in the Reds rotation, but unless he regains lost dominance, Abbott's ratios are vulnerable, particularly at home in Great American Ballpark.

name: Devin Williams
season_outlook: After four seasons serving as one of baseball's most unhittable relievers -- both his 1.75 ERA and .146 BAA from 2020-23 were easily best in the game -- Williams' 2024 swung his skill set into risk/reward territory. Back issues that plagued him late in 2023 resurfaced during spring training, costing him four months, but upon his return he hardly skipped a beat. Among pitchers with at least 20 IP following his July 28 activation, Williams' 43.2% strikeout rate ranked second, his 14 saves tied for fourth and his .133 BAA ranked 10th. The Yankees acquired him during the winter to take over as their closer, their confidence signaling more ?reward? to his fantasy calculus. If his back issues are indeed behind him, he'll make another run at the position's top spot.

name: Ryan Helsley
season_outlook: Helsley vaulted himself into the elite tier of closers with his performance in 2024. He led the majors with 49 saves, setting the Cardinals franchise record, after previously topping out at 19 saves in 2022. While known for his velocity -- he averages nearly 100 mph on his fastball -- Helsley leaned more heavily on his slider last season to tremendous results. He went without allowing an earned run in two of the final three months, leading to a 1.48 ERA in the second half. The right-hander had a forearm blip as recently as 2023 and there is trade risk in addition to the injury risk in his final year before free agency. As long as he's upright and in St. Louis, Helsley will be locked into the ninth inning, and trade concerns should be marginal since there are few teams for which he wouldn't close if dealt.

name: Merrill Kelly
season_outlook: Kelly's two-year run of success was derailed in 2024 by a teres major strain to his throwing shoulder which put him on the shelf from mid-April to mid-August. Arizona was happy enough with the results and confident enough in the health of his shoulder to exercise Kelly's $7 million club option for the 2025 season. He is such an unusual starting pitcher these days because his traditional fastball was his tertiary pitch by usage rate last season, with Kelly instead emphasizing his cutter and changeup. Kelly, like many pitchers in their mid-30s, has had to adjust his repertoire as his velocity has waned, and the changeup in particular has helped in recent seasons. The changeup to lefties and the slider to righties are his preferred put-away pitches, but his strikeout rate fell to below average last year around his recovery from the shoulder strain.

name: Zack Wheeler
season_outlook: In this era with a dwindling number of aces, Wheeler is a relative rarity. He and teammate Aaron Nola are the only pitchers to have made at least 30 starts and totaled 190-plus IP as many as four times over the past six seasons. Since the beginning of 2019, Wheeler's 2,413 fantasy points rank second, his 108 quality starts first, his 1,024 2/3 innings rank second, his 1,094 strikeouts third, his 3.14 ERA ninth and his 1.07 WHIP 10th. He also set personal bests as a 34-year-old in 2024 with his 2.57 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, .191 BAA and 26 quality starts, further signaling his skill set rating as one of the most stable at the position. Wheeler is a pitcher around whom you build your fantasy team.

name: Aaron Nola
season_outlook: Nola is only a one-time All-Star, with his lone All-Star appearance coming back in 2018. While he may not receive much attention nationally, Nola is one of the game's most dependable arms, having made at least 32 starts in each of the last six full MLB seasons. He shaved almost a run off his ERA in 2024 and fell just three strikeouts short of reaching 200 Ks for the sixth consecutive full season. His knuckle curve remains an excellent swing-and-miss pitch and his four-seamer was more effective last year, as opponents combined to bat just .168 against the offering. The right-hander can get bit by the long ball on occasion, and in fact Nola led the National League in homers allowed last season. That said, he still does so much well and won't turn 32 until June. Until further notice, Nola should be considered one of the best No. 2 starters in baseball.

name: Brady Singer
season_outlook: Singer, a first-round pick by the Royals back in 2018, was traded to the Reds this past November in exchange for Jonathan India and Joey Wiemer. The move from Kansas City to Cincinnati comes with a park downgrade, although it's not as significant as one might suspect, at least not in terms of overall run scoring. Great American Ball Park plays more favorably for power hitting, but Singer's heavy sinker approach should help mitigate that factor, at least in theory. He upped his strikeout rate last season and has shown decent swing-and-miss ability with his breaking pitches, though Singer's strikeout rate has typically hovered around league average. While he should be drafted as a streamer in 2025, Singer could emerge as a more regular option for fantasy managers if new skipper Terry Francona can push the right buttons and protect his leads.

name: Pablo Lopez
season_outlook: Lopez is a legitimate frontline starter in Major League Baseball, if not quite a fantasy ace. The right-hander has been dependable, taking the ball 32 times and reaching 180 innings each of the past three seasons -- the last two with Minnesota. Always stingy with walks, Lopez shaved his walk rate to a career-low 5.3 percent last season, which helped him keep his WHIP below 1.20 for the fifth consecutive campaign. He has five different pitches, all of which can generate whiffs, though his changeup was not as effective in 2024. Regardless, Lopez found his groove in the second half, pitching to a 2.77 ERA in 81.1 innings after the break. While Lopez may not look like a particularly flashy upside pick, he misses enough bats and could easily return to All-Star status. He has often underperformed his estimators, though it's always possible he could have a year where the results beat the peripherals.

name: Jack Flaherty
season_outlook: Flaherty returns to Detroit, where he enjoyed a bounce-back beginning to his 2024, before cooling somewhat after a deadline trade to the Dodgers. Thanks in large part to improved command of his signature slider, his strikeout rate rebounded to near his 2018-19 peak, and he tallied 162 IP, his most in five seasons. Flaherty's 2021-22 injury history might always be a lingering worry, but the improvements he made last season give him good odds of delivering similar numbers this year. He should be selected as a third or fourth fantasy starter in mixed leagues.

name: Ryan Walker
season_outlook: Walker has been in the San Francisco system since being drafted out of Washington State in 2018. He made the slow climb up the organizational ladder as a reliever and finally made the big-league roster in 2023. This past season was the coming-out party, as Walker ended up as the primary closer for the Giants by the end of the season and was one of just two relievers to make at least 75 appearances and work at least 80 innings in 2024. While most pitchers have taken a step backward historically after such a season, Walker could pull a Brad Hand from 2016 and 2017 and repeat his success. Walker's delivery and stuff make it very tough for hitters to square him up, and with the closer job in hand, the right-hander is in great shape for 25-plus saves in 2025.

name: Bryce Miller
season_outlook: Between the addition of a splitter and some good fortune on batted balls as well as in stranding runners, Miller took a huge step forward during his sophomore season. He finished among the top-50 overall players both on our Player Rater as well as in fantasy points scored, and even posted 10 quality starts, a 1.75 ERA and an 0.84 WHIP over his 13 second-half starts. Considering Miller's strand rate placed second, his BABIP sixth and his HR/FB percentage ninth during that latter stretch, regression should be expected as he enters year No. 3. His splitter, however, gives him a more legitimate out pitch, and his control is strong enough that he should cruise his way to a top-40 SP season even if his ratios take a step backwards.

name: Matthew Boyd
season_outlook: Boyd fared remarkably well in his return from June 2023 Tommy John surgery across eight late-season starts and an additional three during the postseason, posting a 2.28 ERA and a 28.2% strikeout rate. Most importantly, both his slider and changeup appeared to have similar life to their pre-surgery models, which was apparently enough for the Cubs to commit $29 million to him across the next two seasons. Boyd's career has reflected much streakiness in terms of his control, and his injury history is a concern. However, so long as he's valued as more of a back-of-your-staff mixed-league type, he's well worth taking a chance.

name: Drew Rasmussen
season_outlook: Following his return from July 2023 elbow surgery -- an internal brace procedure, after he had twice previously had Tommy John surgery -- Rasmussen was eased back into action by the Rays, largely as a reliever. He acclimated himself well to the switch, reflecting spikes in his average fastball velocity and strikeout rate, which offers promise heading into 2025. Rasmussen should return to the Rays rotation to begin the year, but keep in mind that their conservative approach to pitching workloads means the right-hander might be looking at closer to a 120- than a 160-inning workload. Still, he has the skills to be an every-start fantasy option while available if his stuff looks as good in March as it did last September.

name: Tanner Scott
season_outlook: Though his control issues still crop up from time to time, Scott's skills have taken gargantuan steps forward over the past two seasons. Among relievers with at least 100 IP over that time, his 2.04 ERA ranks second, his 188 strikeouts rank fourth, his 69 saves plus holds ranks fifth and his .186 BAA comes in at seventh. Scott has also proven his durability by amassing the fourth-most relief innings over that time (150), something the Dodgers surely valued as they signed him to deepen their already strong late-inning relief corps. While the left-hander brings some volatility in the WHIP category, he should be a premium source of holds and/or saves. He should be one of the first relievers off your draft board once the proven, top-shelf closers are gone.

name: David Bednar
season_outlook: Bednar appeared to be on the precipice of becoming a top-tier closer until his clumsy start to the 2024 season. Bednar posted an 11.70 ERA in the first month of the campaign, including three blown saves in the first two weeks. Bednar then went on to convert his next 11 consecutive chances from May 1 until an oblique injury sent him to the injured list in the middle of the summer. The right-hander returned just before the All-Star break but backslid to an 0-5 record with four blown saves in 11 chances, leading to his demotion from the closer role. By season's end, Bednar's strikeout rate had declined six full percentage points while his walk rate worsened another three percentage points. While Bednar is tentatively expected to return to the ninth in 2025, his hold on the job has to be considered extremely tenuous until he shows his health and command troubles are behind him.

name: Yusei Kikuchi
season_outlook: Kikuchi's surface stats may not interest you much, but the numbers inside the numbers should. Before the trade to Houston at the deadline, Kikuchi was getting plenty of strikeouts with Toronto, but too many of his batted balls were landing safely and he won but four of his 22 starts. Upon acquiring him, the Astros encouraged Kikuchi to adjust his repertoire to throw more sliders and fewer fastballs, and the results were fantastic. The left-hander won half of his 10 starts for Houston while slightly increasing his strikeout rate and lowering his batting average against by more than 80 points. The next challenge for Kikuchi will be to find a way to reduce his home-run rate as he has allowed 25 or more homers in three of the past four seasons. A lower walk rate offsets some of that damage, but the long ball is what has kept his ERA above 4.00 in all but one of his seasons in MLB.

name: Trevor Megill
season_outlook: After Devin Williams was lost for four months due to back issues and neither Abner Uribe nor Joel Payamps proved up to the role, Megill swooped in and converted 20-of-22 save chances, his 99-mph fastball and knuckle curve also making him a strong source of strikeouts. With Williams now in New York, Megill figures to get the first crack at the Brewers' closer job to begin 2025, from which he has the skills to be a solid second-tier fantasy option. His so-so walk rate and penchant for fly balls make him slightly riskier than the position's top-tier names, but he's well worth a selection in the middle rounds.

name: Kodai Senga
season_outlook: Senga's sophomore season in MLB never really got off the ground, as a shoulder strain put him on the shelf to begin the campaign and he strained his calf in his very first start back in July, costing him the rest of the regular season. He returned to make three appearances in the postseason, including a surprise start in Game 1 of the NLCS, pitching a total of five innings. That should have set the right-hander up for a relatively normal offseason, though workload expectations will be difficult to pin down after the lost year. He was able to overcome a high walk rate in his first season with the Mets after the making the jump from Japan. If healthy in 2025, Senga could continue to outperform the estimators thanks to the quality of his repertoire and the league's general discombobulation with his ghost forkball.

name: Jose Berrios
season_outlook: Many drafters will seen Berrios' name and shrug before moving on to search for a player with more upside. Berrios is an old standby entering his 10th major-league season, but he is coming off an impressive 2024 season in which he won 16 games, tied for second in the American League. He has been consistent with his workload, making exactly 32 starts in each of the last six full MLB seasons, though the same can't quite be said for performance after Berrios led the AL in hits and earned runs allowed in a disastrous first full year with Toronto in 2022. That season shows a very real downside, but Berrios has steadied himself and once again looks like a viable if unexciting pick to help round out a fantasy pitching staff in 2025.

name: Emmanuel Clase
season_outlook: Clase is the quintessential example of why fantasy managers shouldn't put too much stock into postseason performance. The regular season's most dominating closer -- his 469 fantasy points were 43 more than the next-closest reliever and his 0.61 ERA was third-best in history among pitchers with at least 50 IP -- he was touched up for two losses, one blown save and a 9.00 ERA across seven October appearances. Chalk that up to a pair of ill-placed sliders and an Aaron Judge wall-scraper, as Clase's 100-mph cutter and slider are otherwise typically next-to-impossible to hit. He's among the best at his craft, and, on a Guardians team sure to be scratching and clawing for W's yet again in 2025, he's as good an investment as closers come.

name: Luis Gil
season_outlook: Gil had a breakout campaign in 2024 with a 3.50 ERA, 1.19 WHIP and 171:77 K:BB across 151.2 innings, which narrowly won him the American League Rookie of the Year Award. The right-hander had a 1.99 ERA through the first two months of the season but labored during the summer months and posted a 4.58 ERA the rest of the way. Walks were a concern during both of those periods -- his 77 walks were the most among all MLB pitchers -- which is hardly a surprise since that was a consistent issue through his minor-league career. Gil showcased his strikeout potential with a 10.1 K/9 and has room for growth with just 36 big-league starts under his belt, but he'll likely need to cut down on the walks in order to stave off regression, let alone take a meaningful step forward in his second full season.

name: Bailey Ober
season_outlook: After giving up eight earned runs over 1.1 innings in his 2024 debut, Ober went on an incredible run in which he went 12-4 with a 3.05 ERA and 0.92 WHIP over 138.1 innings, before hitting the skids again at the end of the season. Overall, it was an impressive showing for the 6-foot-9 righty as he solidified his standing in the middle of the Minnesota rotation. He has four quality pitches and his strikeout and walk rates are good enough to make up for the occasional bout of gopheritis. The disappointing end to the season (0-4, 5.59 ERA in his final seven starts) may be enough to keep the more casual drafters away, but the secret is out amongst the wider drafting public. Chances are, the home runs will persist given his flyball tendencies, but Ober is good enough to overcome them and reach double-digit wins once again for a competitive Twins team.

name: MacKenzie Gore
season_outlook: Not often are 26-year-olds asked to front pitching rotations, but that is where Gore finds himself with Washington entering the 2025 season. Gore has made 59 starts for the Nationals since arriving from San Diego as part of the Juan Soto deal, and he made good strides in his second season with the organization. Gore increased his workload by 30 innings while reducing his HR/9 from 1.8 to 0.8, throwing with more velocity and posting a sub-4.00 ERA for the first time in his career. He got to double-digit wins, but the 3.90 ERA and 1.42 WHIP do not go together, with the latter implying Gore was fortunate when it came to run prevention. It's reasonable to be picking up Mitch Keller vibes here because the similarities in their career paths are a bit uncanny. Whether or not Gore can shoulder a 180-plus-inning workload is the lingering question.

name: Chris Bassitt
season_outlook: Bassitt's ERA last year was half a run higher than the previous season, while his 1.46 WHIP in 2024 was the second highest among qualified starters. Bassitt's walk rate was his highest since 2018, but the bigger culprit was a .333 BABIP, third highest among all qualifiers. A bloated hit rate can be misfortune, but it can also be a sign of a pitcher being more hittable. Bassitt's strikeout rate is a tick below league average, so he needs to minimize traffic to be effective. Bassitt's track record warrants the benefit of the doubt, but he'll be 36 years old this season, so a full rebound will be challenging. Pitching in the AL East isn't conducive to favorable matchups, relegating Bassitt to deep leagues, at least until he demonstrates a return to his previous control levels.

name: Seth Lugo
season_outlook: After several years spent toiling in mediocrity between the rotation and bullpen, Lugo enjoyed a surprise breakout at 34 years old in his first season as a member of the Royals' rotation. He was a first-time All-Star and won 16 games, tied for second in the American League. Lugo surged past 200 innings for the first time ever after previously topping out at 146.1 frames in 2023. It's rather tough to buy into given Lugo's lack of strikeouts or track record, but he has one of the best defenses in the majors behind him. The righty had nine different pitches categorized by Statcast last season, and that ability to throw the kitchen sink helps keep opposing hitters off balance and off his four-seam fastball. He may be a fade for some, but it's possible Lugo found something with Kansas City that will allow him to continue beating the estimators in 2025.

name: Nathan Eovaldi
season_outlook: Eovaldi went a long way in shedding the fragility label by throwing his second-highest innings total last season. He will miss a start from time to time, as he has but twice made 30 starts, but when he is out there, he works deep into games thanks to his ability to throw four different pitches to lefties and five to righties. The repertoire is a bit susceptible to the long ball, but Eovaldi's stinginess with walks offsets the damage from those homers. He is one of just six pitchers to have posted an ERA of 4.00 and a WHIP below 1.25 while pitching at least 100 innings in each of the past four seasons, joining the likes of Framber Valdez, Corbin Burnes, Kevin Gausman, Logan Webb and Zack Wheeler. That's good company to keep.

name: Felix Bautista
season_outlook: Recovery from Tommy John surgery cost Bautista the entirety of 2024, but baseball is expected to have its best reliever (at the time of the operation) back in time to close for the Orioles come Opening Day. In 2023, he registered the sixth-best strikeout rate (46.4%) of any pitcher with at least 60 IP, and became only the eighth pitcher in history with at least 30 saves, 110 strikeouts and a sub-1.50 ERA. Whether Bautista's raw stuff will approach those heights in his first season back following surgery is a fair question, but perhaps his spring training might provide some hints. All signs point to his being worthy of a top-five selection at his position in fantasy leagues regardless.

name: Brandon Woodruff
season_outlook: Woodruff looked like a rising star for Milwaukee not long ago, earning All-Star selections in 2019 and 2021. However, he has missed the better part of two seasons due to injury, including all of 2024, after undergoing surgery in October of 2023 to repair the anterior capsule in his right shoulder. While the Brewers will not commit to Woodruff being ready for Opening Day 2025, he was said to be in a good spot and throwing multiple bullpen sessions per week in January. Entering his age-32 season, Woodruff is a wild card for both the Brewers and fantasy managers. The innings floor is zilch and the workload ceiling is capped, but Woodruff's excellent track record of performance (career 3.10 ERA, 1.05 WHIP) will likely tempt some to roll the dice outside the top 200 picks or so overall.

name: Sandy Alcantara
season_outlook: Alcantara, the Cy Young Award winner in the National League in 2022, missed all of last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery in October of 2023. He advanced from regular side sessions to throwing live batting practice last September and will be nearly 18 months removed from the procedure by the time Opening Day rolls around. The Marlins have not publicly disclosed an innings target for Alcantara in 2025, but somewhere around 150 frames likes a good starting point, with room for more if his arm holds up. The injury concerns are not going away anytime soon with a pitcher that throws so hard, but if he proves healthy after the long layoff, Alcantara could prove to be a bargain for fantasy managers at his average draft position. Expect the acquisition cost to rise considerably if Alcantara is pumping gas and looking healthy in spring training.

name: Spencer Schwellenbach
season_outlook: His status as a shortstop/closer during his college days at Nebraska, coupled with the 2021 Tommy John surgery that delayed the start of his professional career, perhaps allowed Schwellenbach to sneak beneath the radar entering 2024. The Braves, desperate for rotation options, gave him a look in late May, despite his having only made two starts as high as Double-A ball at the time. He never looked back. Schwellenbach finished 16th among starting pitchers in fantasy points, thanks to his five solid pitch offerings and an elite walk rate (his 4.6% ranked in the 95th percentile). While he's likely to regress somewhat as the league becomes more familiar with him, he has the skills to remain a top-40 fantasy starter if given the innings (he totaled 168 2/3 between the majors and minors in 2024).

name: Nick Lodolo
season_outlook: Through three injury-riddled seasons, Lodolo's ERA is 4.52, but his xFIP is 3.74 with a 3.53 SIERA. After posting a 29% strikeout rate over his first two seasons, it fell to 24.7% last season, but Lodolo was dealing with lingering effects from a stress reaction in his left tibia, a groin strain and finger issues. His velocity was up from 2023, but he didn't generate as many swinging strikes from his curve and changeup, while increasing sinker usage, which is designed to induce groundballs and not swing and misses. Still just 27 years old, if Lodolo can shake the injury bug, he can become the pitcher teased by his ERA estimators. The risk is worth the reward to hope he finally realizes his potential.

name: Mitch Keller
season_outlook: Keller took a significant step forward in 2023, setting career highs across the board, and the Pirates rewarded him with a five-year contract extension prior to last season. He then went onto post similar if slightly disappointing numbers in 2024, as his strikeout rate declined four percentage points and both his ERA and WHIP worsened a bit from the previous season. Keller's average fastball velocity dropped about one mile per hour, and every little bit counts when it comes to velocity. His four-seamer saw the most damage of the fastballs as the league hit 80 points better against that pitch. The right-hander is one of just 13 pitchers to throw at least 175 innings each of the past two seasons and Pittsburgh will be leaning on him to stabilize a young rotation in 2025.

name: Cade Smith
season_outlook: Smith emerged from relative obscurity last season to become one of the top arms in the Cleveland bullpen, pitching to a sparkling 1.91 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and 103:17 K:BB over 75.1 innings. Despite notching just one save, Smith outearned many closers in standard scoring, including Kenley Jansen and Jhoan Duran among others. His walk rates on the farm suggest he could give back some of his gains in that particular department, but Smith looks here to stay given that he has three dominant pitches in his four-seamer, splitter and sweeper. At 25 years old, Smith is already a remarkable success story, having signed with the Guardians as an undrafted free agent in 2020. Emmanuel Clase is standing in his way of regular save chances, but Smith looks like closer material in the long term, and in the short term he will be highly coveted in leagues scoring holds.

name: Roki Sasaki
season_outlook: The most anticipated Japanese hurler in seven seasons, Sasaki makes the jump to MLB after four seasons of a 2.02 ERA and a 32.4% strikeout rate overseas, which included a 19-strikeout perfect game in 2022. Though his velocity dipped slightly in 2024, he made 18 starts and had 10 wins, a 2.35 ERA, a 1.04 WHIP and a 28.7% K rate. Sasaki should immediately slot into the Dodgers rotation with prospective top-10 fantasy value in each start he makes. The primary questions surrounding him are health- and workload-related. Can he blow past 100 IP and secure his place as one of fantasy baseball's premier starters? Or will 2025 serve a stepping stone to a future claim of that status over the next couple of years? Either way, Sasaki should be selected in the middle rounds of 2025 drafts. He's a 23-year-old building block in all dynasty and keeper formats.

name: Ryan Pepiot
season_outlook: The primary return for the Rays in the Tyler Glasnow trade, Pepiot slotted directly into the team's rotation with a productive, top-60 SP fantasy season. Most notably, he rebounded from multiple IL stints due to fluky circumstances (a leg injury after being struck by a liner, a bug bite that led to a knee infection) to set professional bests in starts and innings pitched as well as a 2.95 ERA and 25.7% strikeout rate across his final nine starts. It sets Pepiot up for another similarly, if not a couple of tiers better, productive 2025. Now, the Rays' move to George M. Steinbrenner Field will set him back from a park factor perspective and the team's tendency to mix and match on the pitching side might prevent a big innings bump. Even so, he's a solid fourth or fifth mixed-league starter.

name: Corbin Burnes
season_outlook: How you regard Burnes might come down to these conflicting thoughts: Is his precipitous, four-year pattern of declining strikeout rates worrisome, or does the Diamondbacks' six-year, $210 million commitment to the right-hander strengthen confidence in his skills? The answer might lie somewhere in between. Burnes and Logan Webb are the only pitchers with at least 95 starts, 60 quality starts and 590 IP over the past three seasons. That durailbity, combined with his repertoire tweaks -- he's increasingly going for minimizing hard contact rather than for swings and misses -- diminish the instinct to panic about possible skills erosion. Burnes might no longer be a Cy Young favorite, but he looks the part of dependable top-10 fantasy starting pitcher.

name: Gavin Williams
season_outlook: In hindsight, Williams' 2024 appeared to be a significant step backward, as an elbow injury cost him the season's first three months and his ERA ballooned by nearly a run and a half. Still, he added nearly a full tick of velocity to his fastball, and his curveball served as a legitimate swing-and-miss offering. The ingredients remain here for Williams to develop into one of fantasy's better starters, though he does have work to do before earning draft status as such. Consider him in the final rounds of 12-team mixed leagues, particularly if he's looking good come March.

name: Pete Fairbanks
season_outlook: Rays manager Kevin Cash has a reputation for spreading the wealth when it comes to save chances, but Fairbanks has been the skipper's go-to arm in the ninth inning when available over the past two seasons. Fairbanks recorded 20-plus saves for the second straight year before a right lat strain ended his 2024 season, adding another chapter to his sketchy health history. Even with all the injuries in his career, Fairbanks continues to pump gas with 93rd percentile fastball velocity, though that didn't translate to many strikeouts in 2024. For now, Fairbanks can still be considered Tampa Bay's primary closer, but that run could be coming to an end in the not-too-distant future given his price tag for 2026 and the fact that he has incentives based on games finished in 2025.

name: Bryan Abreu
season_outlook: Abreu is the only reliever in baseball to have struck out 100 or more batters out of the bullpen in each of the past two seasons, joining teammate Josh Hader as well as Fernando Cruz and Mason Miller in that club for 2024. Abreu could challenge for saves on most other clubs, but as long as he and Hader are teammates, Abreu appears to be the Robin to Hader's Batman. Abreu has the highest strikeout rate among all non-closing relievers over the past three seasons, and those strikeouts and stellar ratios make Abreu an interesting play in deep formats. The risk comes in the fact that so few relievers ever work 70-plus innings over consecutive seasons let alone three as Abreu will likely be asked to do with Houston dealing Ryan Pressly away this winter.

name: Ryan Pressly
season_outlook: Pressly signed a two-year deal with the Astros in April of 2022 with a vesting option for 2025, which included a full no-trade clause. After much speculation, Pressly waived that no-trade clause in January to facilitate a move to the Cubs, for whom he's expected to close in 2025. His fantasy outlook is significantly brighter now after Pressly took a back seat to Josh Hader throughout 2024. Pressly is coming off a season in which his fastball continued its decline, putting even more pressure on the right-hander to effectively execute his breaking pitches. This past season saw Pressly's strikeout rate fall below 25 percent for the first time since 2017, and he will likely face competition for saves eventually from Porter Hodge and others in the Chicago bullpen.

name: Kyle Finnegan
season_outlook: Strictly in terms of shutting the door and securing wins for his team, Finnegan has been one of the top closers in baseball over the past couple years. In fact, only Emmanuel Clase, Josh Hader and Raisel Iglesias have more saves than Finnegan since the start of the 2023 season. However, he lacks the swing-and-miss dominance typically associated with the late innings. The Nationals declined to tender Finnegan a contract for 2025 despite his success, making him a free agent in November. Finnegan reined in the long ball and did not allow a single homer over the final two months of last season, but it seems more likely than not that he's without a closer job to begin 2025 since the underlying numbers are not closer-worthy. His experience and success in the ninth should keep him on your radar, but at best he's a speculative endgame pick until there's clarity on his situation.

name: Taj Bradley
season_outlook: After struggling with home runs and the command of his fastball as a rookie, Bradley made big strides in 2024 that bode well for his future. He boosted his ground-ball rate by 6%, added more than 2% to his whiff rate, and rattled off a final 20 starts in which his ERA was 3.71 and he generated MLB's 11th-most strikeouts (122). Considering Bradley's prospect status, it was a signal that he might begin to realize his future ace potential in 2025. The Rays do tend to take a conservative approach with their young starters' innings, and their move from pitchers' heaven Tropicana Field to George M. Steinbrenner Field sets them back slightly. Still, Bradley should be drafted in the middle rounds based upon his upside.

name: Sean Manaea
season_outlook: After teasing fantasy managers for years with encouraging underlying metrics but so-so results, a tweak to his mechanics in late July finally spawned a breakthrough for Manaea. By lowering his arm angle, he added three full percentage points to his whiff rate and 6% to his ground-ball percentage across his final 12 regular-season starts, during which he had three double-digit strikeout games, a 3.09 ERA, a 28.4% K rate and the second-most fantasy points among pitchers (202). Whether Manaea can maintain those gains is a fair question as he had never before 2024 posted a full-season ERA lower than 3.50, but there's certainly top-40 SP potential here with the tweaks taken into account. He's worth a quick spring re-examination before investing at that price point, but his arrow is pointing upward.

name: Brayan Bello
season_outlook: After inking the right-hander to a six-year contract extension in early March, Boston rolled out the red carpet for Bello on Opening Day, and Bello even pitched like a frontline starter for a brief stretch. Ultimately, his numbers resembled those of a back-end starter. His season was interrupted by a lat injury in late April which necessitated a trip to the injured list, and Bello found himself struggling with walks upon his return, issuing three or more free passes 10 times following his activation in May. His overall walk rate was 9.1 percent, and that is walking a fine line when the pitcher has a strikeout rate barely above 20 percent for their career. Bello generally does a good job of keeping the ball in the park with his sinker-slider-changeup mix, though lefties can touch him up. Fantasy managers should approach Bello with caution as he attempts to navigate the tough AL East once again in 2025.

name: Jameson Taillon
season_outlook: Taillon had a surprising return to his halcyon days this past season, winning 12 of his 28 starts and pitching to the best ERA of his career. No new pitch was added nor was any one pitch thrown that much more than it was in 2023, but the sweeper performed better in 2024. Taillon does what many pitchers without big fastballs do, choosing to throw six different pitches rather than honing in on a smaller collection of pitches. He usually manages to keep hitters off-balance by throwing four of his six offerings at least 15 percent of the time. He continued to lag in the strikeout department last season -- his strikeout rate was several clicks below the league average for starting pitchers -- so he will have to continue to rely upon batted-ball fortunes to keep his ERA out of the danger zone.

name: Bowden Francis
season_outlook: A strong spring earned Francis a spot in the Blue Jays' Opening Day rotation, but an 8.59 ERA and 1.70 WHIP after five starts earned him a trip to Triple-A Buffalo. Francis returned in early June to pitch out of the bullpen and fared a bit better, posting a 4.13 ERA and 1.33 WHIP in 24 frames before he was sent back down. Francis was recalled in late July and something clicked, as he registered a 1.80 ERA and 0.60 WHIP in 65 frames. A .142 BABIP and 95.5 percent left-on-base rate indicate a stretch good luck, though the strikeout and walk numbers also show that Francis pitched better. He used fewer fastballs and changeups while throwing more splitters and breaking pitches. Trusting the small sample to end the season is a slippery slope, but Francis' skill improvement merits taking the chance at cost.

name: Justin Martinez
season_outlook: Martinez began the season with Triple-A Reno, but after punching out 14 hitters in 6.2 innings, he was called up in mid-April. Early on, he worked in low-leverage scenarios, notching his first hold June 4. Martinez then serves as a setup man until August when he took over as the primary closer for Arizona. He converted eight of nine chances over the final two months and Martinez has stuff to continue closing as he averages triple digits on his four-seam fastball and sinker, though can struggle to locate on occasion. His WHIP will be high with the walks, so saves will come with ratio baggage. Just 23 years old, Martinez can certainly learn to throw more strikes. He'll enter the season as the favorite for saves in the desert, though A.J. Puk looms if Martinez's control issues yield too many blown saves.

name: Luke Weaver
season_outlook: Weaver's first season exclusively working out of the bullpen went swimmingly as he tied for third among relievers with 103 strikeouts in 2024. He added velocity to his fastball and cutter and used them more while reducing the usage of his slider and knuckle-curve. Weaver spent most of the season in a setup capacity, often throwing more than one inning before taking over as the Yankees closer down the stretch and into the playoffs, and he finished the campaign with four saves and 23 holds. Even so, the Yankees traded for Devin Williams, pushing Weaver back to garnering holds, though he's still likely to pick up the odd save, along with supporting ratios and strikeouts.

name: Shane Baz
season_outlook: Baz began the season with Triple-A Durham, starting 10 games but only logging 39.1 innings. After being called up in early July, Baz started 14 games spanning 79.1 frames. His 3.06 ERA with the Rays looks effective, but a 4.39 xFIP and 4.33 SIERA paint a different picture. Baz's strikeout rate was way down while his walk rate was up relative to his pre-injury levels. Throwing 118.2 combined innings last season suggests Baz can handle a bump into the 150-170 range, and considering that he was able to reach back for more zip at times last season, it's reasonable to think he may be able to add velocity  in 2025. A return to pre-injury form and the top of the rotation is in play, but don't expect ace production right away.

name: Justin Steele
season_outlook: Steele followed up his breakout season with very similar numbers around stints on the injured list with hamstring and elbow issues. His ERA and strikeout rate were nearly identical to his 2023 marks while his 1.10 WHIP was by far a career best. The left-hander returned from his elbow injury to make a couple starts for the Cubs at the end of the campaign, but they were abbreviated starts, and for many the dark cloud of uncertainty follows Steele into 2025. Among the 46 pitchers that have totaled 300 innings over the past two seasons, Steele ranks 16th in strikeout-minus-walk percentage, which demonstrates a high-end skills foundation. If he can stay healthy, Steele could ascend to legitimate ace status, but until he adds that missing piece, drafters should proceed with a degree of caution.

name: Zack Littell
season_outlook: Littell's 29 starts and 156.1 innings last season were personal highs. His strikeout-minus-walk percentage of 16.8 percent was a career best, which is even more impressive since last season was his first as a full-time starter. He was snake bit with a .311 BABIP, as his line-drive rate was abnormally high. Littell is due regression in that area, which should in theory improve his WHIP. However, Littell's home-run rate has been above average in Tropicana Field, and it's in danger of rising even more at Steinbrenner Field. Littell remains a matchup play, though he loses some appeal for home games in 2025.

name: Lucas Erceg
season_outlook: Erceg earned his first three career saves with the A's last year and added 14 more with the Royals following a deadline trade, including three during the postseason. He reached a whole new level after the move to Kansas City, pitching to a 2.88 ERA, 0.84 WHIP and 31:3 K:BB across his final 25 regular-season innings. Overall, Erceg threw 67.2 frames around a brief stint on the injured list with forearm tightness. The control he displayed was shocking given his walk rates had consistently been above five per nine since he made the transition from third base to the pitching mound in 2021. While he's been traded twice in recent years and lacks any track record of success beyond last season, Erceg has the high-end fastball velocity and swing-and-miss secondaries to maintain the closer role throughout 2025, if he can keep the walks in check.

name: Tanner Houck
season_outlook: Houck unlocked a new level last season and solidified his spot in the Boston rotation heading into 2025.
