He was one of the stories of the first half, pitching to a brilliant 2.54 ERA across his first 19 starts en route to his first All-Star selection. However, the right-hander eventually hit the wall. Manager Alex Cora noted that Houck was essentially pitching through a dead arm phase down the stretch, which makes sense given that Houck had previously spent time in the bullpen and maxed out at a little over 100 innings the year prior. With 178.2 frames in 2024, Houck ranked second on the team, and the Red Sox will be hoping he can handle a similar workload this season. The division is brutal and his strikeout rate is modest, but Houck does a good job of keeping the ball on the ground with his sweeper-sinker-splitter combo.

name: Nick Martinez
season_outlook: After serving in a swingman capacity for a couple of years, Martinez is slated to be a full-time starter in 2025. Last season, Martinez started 16 times with 26 relief appearances. His numbers as a reliever were better than as a starter (1.86 ERA relief vs. a 3.84 in the rotation), so he'll be challenged to repeat last year's 3.10 ERA and 1.03 WHIP working out of the Reds' rotation, especially with a below average strikeout rate. Martinez has a starter's arsenal, featuring a four-seam fastball, cutter, sinker and changeup with the occasional curve and slider. Last season's success was driven by a stingy 3.2% walk rate, which he'll be hard-pressed to repeat. Historically, Martinez has been a groundball pitcher, but last season he allowed more flyballs than grounders, though he yielded only 13 homers in 142 1/3 innings. Especially at home, Martinez's success will revolve around his ability to keep the ball in the yard. It's tempting to trust last season's breakthrough, but the paucity of punchouts and likely homer regression tempers expectations.

name: Michael Wacha
season_outlook: Wacha has pitched for four different teams over the past four years, but he has found a home in Kansas City after his best season since 2015 which earned him a new three-year contract. Indeed, Wacha's numbers are impressive for a pitcher who does not exactly blow hitters away. The right-hander throws the kitchen sink at righties and lefties, serving up six different offerings to be exact, led by his great changeup. The addition of a slider in 2024 gave him two different shapes to his breaking ball to go along with the changeup and three fastball variations. What a pitcher lacks in velocity they have to make up for in pitch execution and craftiness, and Wacha is quite adept at both these days. He's no ace, but Wacha can help stabilize real and fantasy rotations.

name: Jason Adam
season_outlook: Adam has been on a three-year tear since being plucked by the Rays off the free-agent wire when the Cubs didn't see what they had. He has shown the ability to step in for saves when needed as well as contribute to all five pitching categories. Adam's success comes from his ability to throw four different pitch types to both righties and lefties, and he will use any of his pitches at any time. This past season saw him improve his slider which was downright unhittable. Adam's .162 batting average against over the past three seasons leads all relievers with at least 150 innings pitched over that span, and he is 10 points lower than any other pitcher on that list. Robert Suarez is still the favorite for saves in San Diego, but Adam has value as a late-inning weapon and his value skyrockets should anything happen with Suarez.

name: Alexis Diaz
season_outlook: Control has always been an issue for Diaz, but he fanned over 30 percent of the batters he faced in his first two seasons, so he was able to get away with a high walk rate. Last season, Diaz's walk rate remained high, but his strikeout rate plummeted to 22.7 percent. He still saved 28 games in 32 chances, but his ratios were high, and his 55 strikeouts were the third fewest among relievers that logged at least 25 saves. Diaz only throws a four-seam fastball and slider, and last season his fastball velocity dipped for the second straight season. His swinging-strike rate also fell for the second consecutive year. The trends are a bit troubling, but Diaz could still regain some fastball zip. There isn't anyone to immediately challenge Diaz for saves and new manager Terry Francona historically prefers a set closer, but Diaz's job security can't be considered high until he regains dominance.

name: Grayson Rodriguez
season_outlook: Shoulder and lat issues thwarted Rodriguez's chances at a major breakthrough in 2024. Coming off a 2023 second half in which he posted a 2.58 ERA, he was held to just 20 starts with noticeably diminished raw stuff. Long forecasted as a front-of-the-rotation arm, Rodriguez (when healthy) can reach 100 mph while averaging 97 mph with his fastball, along with a plus slider and changeup. Last season, however, his velocity was down a tick, his ground ball rate dropped, and he posted a 4.86 ERA across his final eight starts. All indications are that Rodriguez's lat issues are behind him entering spring training, however, and he's young enough to get immediately back on track as one of the game's most promising starters. He'll warrant a closer look once spring games begin, but there's enough potential here to make him a top-40 fantasy starter, even accounting for the health risk.

name: Zach Eflin
season_outlook: The Rays, as they are wont to do, flipped Eflin last summer after building up his value. Eflin was better than ever after his move to Baltimore, going 5-2 with a 2.60 ERA in nine starts down the stretch in the regular season after failing to replicate the success he had with Tampa Bay in 2023 prior to the trade. While Eflin does not have overpowering stuff, he keeps hitters off balance with six different pitches and is ultra stingy with walks. An 88th percentile chase rate suggests he could rebound a bit in the strikeout department in 2025. The team context is generally favorable, but keep in mind that the Orioles are moving in the left-field wall at Camden Yards, and pitching in the AL East is no piece of cake. With that, it's probably best to view Eflin as a pitcher that will be in and out of weekly lineups.

name: Shane McClanahan
season_outlook: On the mend from his second career Tommy John surgery -- his first was in college in 2016, while this one was in August 2023 -- McClanahan should be eased back into the rotation gently by the always cautious Rays. Before the operation, he had developed into one of the game's best at his craft, with his 3.02 ERA and 33.4% whiff rates both ranking top-10 among pitchers with at least 50 starts from 2021-23. Whether McClanahan can quickly snap back to those levels is unclear, but if he's looking good during spring training and on track for the Opening Day rotation, he'd be a potential top-30 fantasy starter.

name: Griffin Jax
season_outlook: Few relievers made as many gains in 2024 as Jax. He added more than a half-mph to his average fastball velocity, significantly boosted the whiff rate on his sweeper and lowered his walk rate to 5.4%, with the result being the 10th-highest fantasy point total among relief pitchers (closers or middle relief). Jax thrived in his eighth-inning role, additionally securing 10 saves, and in most every regard outperformed closer Jhoan Duran in the process. That's not to say that a closer competition is destined this spring, but considering manager Rocco Baldelli's preference for matchups-oriented relief roles, Jax should put forth meaningful, nearly top-10 RP fantasy stats, regardless of how he's used.

name: Ronel Blanco
season_outlook: Blanco became the talk of the baseball world when he tossed a no-hitter April 1 against the Blue Jays, one of three individual no-hitters in the majors last season. He was then ejected from a start in May after a substance check on his glove which led to an automatic 10-game suspension. The right-hander continued to pitch well following his return from suspension with a 3.07 ERA and 1.10 WHIP over his final 120 regular-season innings for the Astros. While his underlying numbers paint a picture of good fortune, it was still a highly impressive season. Late bloomers often fizzle as quickly as they pop onto the scene, but the 31-year-old Blanco looks here to stay if he can keep the walks in check. He averaged roughly a strikeout per inning in his first full season in the Houston rotation.

name: Charlie Morton
season_outlook: Though his advancing age (he's now 41) continues to chip away at his skills, Morton keeps on returning modest mixed-league value with good durability. He's one of only four pitchers who has made at least 30 starts in each of the last six complete MLB seasons (Jose Berrios, Patrick Corbin, Aaron Nola) and even in a 2024 in which he posted his fewest fantasy points in any of those years (286), he still placed 62nd at his position. Morton should continue to pile up innings while flashing respectable ratios, making him a worthwhile back-of-your-staff type.

name: Camilo Doval
season_outlook: Doval tied for the National League lead in saves in 2023 when he racked up 39, but he pitched his way out of the closer role last season and even off the major-league roster for a stretch in August. The right-hander lost his feel for the strike zone, posting the second-highest walk percentage among qualifying relievers at 14.4 percent. Doval wasn't much better in that regard following his return from Triple-A, handing out 10 free passes in his final 13 big-league innings. Ryan Walker took over the ninth inning for the Giants when Doval was demoted and seems likely to have the inside track on the closer job in 2025 given his success down the stretch last season. That doesn't mean Doval can't return to the closer role, as he has electric stuff, but he probably still has some work to do to regain the trust of manager Bob Melvin.

name: Luis Severino
season_outlook: Severino and the rest of the Athletics will be playing their home games at Sutter Health Park in West Sacramento this season, in a park that will also remain home to the Triple-A Sacramento River Cats of the Pacific Coast League. The move does not bode well for the pitching staff, at least not on paper, but this is what Severino signed up for when he inked a three-year deal in December. The right-hander rebounded with the Mets in 2024, clearing 30 starts for the first time since 2018 as one of nine pitchers in the National League to exceed 180 innings last season. Severino still throws hard for a starting pitcher, but his strikeout rate has fallen precipitously in recent years, from above 35 percent at his peak to just 21.1 percent last season. The team context and questionable upside will drive many away.

name: Jared Jones
season_outlook: Jones rode a stellar spring training into a spot in the Pirates' Opening Day rotation, then was one of baseball's most productive rookies for nearly three months. Through June 22, his nine quality starts paced his freshman class, and his 93 K's were second to only eventual AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil. Unfortunately, a right lat strain cost Jones nearly eight weeks shortly thereafter, and he was inexplicably more reliant upon his curveball (his worst-performing pitch) for the rest of the way. Between Jones' quiet finish, and the presence of burgeoning superstar Paul Skenes within the same rotation, Jones might come at a relative discount entering 2025. His upside can't match that of Skenes, but Jones could be ready to take a step forward into the top-40 SP conversation.

name: Reynaldo Lopez
season_outlook: When Lopez signed with Atlanta, he said he wanted another chance to be a starter. Lopez had evolved into a dominant reliever during the 2023 season, so the move back to the rotation was odd with the last laugh coming at the expense of the non-believers. Lopez, before his body encouraged him to shut things down, had a phenomenal season, striking out more than a batter an inning while reducing both his walk and home-run rates from previous seasons. None of this came from any new pitch, but rather Lopez rediscovered his potential with better pitch execution. Lopez comes into 2025 as the second-most tenured arm on the staff by age and major-league experience. His close to the season with shoulder inflammation is concerning since he just doubled his workload last season and will be asked for more in 2025.

name: Gerrit Cole
season_outlook: Relative to the six seasons that preceded it (as well as to the first-round draft valuation he had earned for much of the past half-decade), Cole's 2024 will be regarded by most as a colossal disappointment. But considering the elbow injury that shelved him from mid-March through mid-June could have been a lot worse -- Tommy John fears were very real when it first cropped up -- Cole's late-season recovery offered room for future hope. While his average fastball velocity never quite reached pre-injury levels (a 95.9 mph average, down from 97.3 over his first four Yankees seasons), he posted a 2.25 ERA and a 26.0% strikeout rate across his final 10 regular-season starts. That was followed by a quintet of serviceable, if unextraordinary, playoff outings (a 2.17 ERA, but six unearned runs). Cole's health bears watching throughout spring training, but with no trip-ups, he should have another top-10 SP season in his talented right arm.

name: Jeffrey Springs
season_outlook: Springs debuted in late July following rehab from Tommy John surgery. He started seven games before being shut down for the season with left elbow fatigue in mid-September. His fastball was down a tick (velocity usually returns quickly), but the strikeout rate was in line with his pre-injury numbers. Springs walk rate was higher than normal, but diminished command immediately after returning is expected, especially since his signature pitch is a changeup which is slower to come around. The Athletics must have been encouraged by Springs' performance as they acquired the 32-year-old southpaw in December. Including rehab, the lefty totaled 65 innings, so expecting more than 120 frames in 2025 is aggressive. Springs is generally a matchup option, but that approach is clouded with the uncertainty of how Sutter Health Park in Sacramento will play.

name: Nestor Cortes
season_outlook: Nasty Nestor will be taking his talents to Milwaukee in 2025, having come over from The Bronx in the Devin Williams trade. Cortes was the Opening Day starter for the Yankees last season and ended up making 30 starts for the first time in his career before landing on the injured list with a left elbow flexor strain. After acquiring Cortes, the Brewers said that the lefty was full healthy and enjoying a normal offseason despite the late injury. Since his breakout with New York a few years back, Cortes has proven plenty capable as a major-league starter, and his new organization has had success developing and revitalizing arms in their pitching lab. Fantasy managers should just be hoping for a repeat in 2025, though it's not completely out of the question that the team could help Cortes find a new level as he competes in a weaker division.

name: Jeremiah Estrada
season_outlook: Estrada was a fantasy sleeper for a couple of years, but after he punched out 13 hitters in a row last May, everyone's eyes were wide open. He proceeded to post an impressive campaign, helping the Padres make the postseason. Once the Cubs' closer of the future, the 26-year-old righty could be in line to fulfill that destiny with the Padres, though he'll have to wait with Robert Suarez slated for ninth-inning duties and Jason Adam next in line as the primary setup man. Still, Estrada will garner high-leverage work and has a chance to join the 100-strikeout club while racking up holds.

name: A.J. Puk
season_outlook: Given a four-start opportunity in the Marlins rotation, Puk struggled mightily and ultimately missed three weeks due to shoulder problems at the onset of 2024. Upon his return, he flourished when restored to his former bullpen role, including a 1.41 ERA, two saves, 13 holds and a 38.6% strikeout rate from June forward, scarcely even affected by his deadline trade to the Diamondbacks. Puk should again be one of the top arms in the Arizona bullpen, perhaps even ending up in the mix for save chances. Whether he handles the eighth or ninth inning, he should be one of the first 20 relievers off your draft board.

name: Kirby Yates
season_outlook: Here's how good Yates' rebound 2024 was: He became only the second pitcher in history to post multiple seasons of at least 60 IP with a sub-1.20 ERA (Wade Davis, 2014-15). His shift to an effectively two-pitch repertoire of high fastballs and low splitters not only restored his status as one of the game's most effective relievers, but also earned him a $13 million free agent contract with the Dodgers. Whether it's saves or holds he's getting from the team's matchup-oriented bullpen, Yates should be one of the better picks at his position. His drawbacks are less about skills and more about his age (he's 38) and injury history (four IL stints since the beginning of 2020).

name: Jake Irvin
season_outlook: Irvin's 33 starts tied for most in the majors last season, as he pitched a career-high 187.2 innings. His 4.41 ERA was a tad high according to a 4.03 xFIP and 4.21 SIERA. With a low 20.3 percent strikeout rate, Irvin is more susceptible to variance, which is amplified by a high home run rate. Irvin improved his strikeout and walk rates last season and is just 28 years old, so he could continue to improve. The Nationals are also developing something of a reputation for developing pitching. The safe play is paying for the floor and deploying Irvin sagely, avoiding power-laden lineups.

name: Grant Holmes
season_outlook: A decently regarded prospect back in his Dodgers/Athletics days nearly a decade ago, Holmes finally reached the majors last June at the age of 28, parlaying his elite control and whiff-generating slider and curveball into a swingman role with the Braves. His performance impressed them enough that he earned the start in their must-win Game 162 against the Mets, in which he tossed four shutout innings of 1-hit, 7-K baseball, and winter chatter had him as a likely member of their 2025 Opening Day rotation. Whether Holmes, who before last season's 109 1/3 combined innings between the majors and minors hadn't exceeded 90 frames since 2017, has the stamina to hold up to a full-season starter's role is in question, but he's an intriguing flier in deep mixed and NL-only formats.

name: Clarke Schmidt
season_outlook: Although a lat strain cost him more than three months of time, Schmidt's 2024 reflected important signs of growth. He boosted his innings-per-start average by 0.38 and his K rate by nearly 5%. He also lowered his wOBA against lefties by nearly 70 points compared to 2023, and he was allowed to throw 100-plus pitches five times, his first such starts as a major leaguer. Schmidt still needs to add stamina in order to reach the upper tier of fantasy starters, but his incremental gains year over year bode well for his taking another step in 2025. Consider him in the mid-to-late rounds in mixed leagues deeper than ESPN's standard.

name: Matt Strahm
season_outlook: Strahm has really found himself in the Philadelphia bullpen over the last two seasons, emerging as one of the National League's top lefty setup options. He shortened up last season and turned in a career year, earning his first All-Star selection at 32 years old. Not only did Strahm cut his home-run rate in half last season, he also improved his strikeout and walk rates en route to the third-best strikeout-to-walk ratio among regular relievers (7.18). While his fastball is lacking in terms of velocity, he nevertheless enjoys great results with the pitch, and his slider induces a good amount of swing and miss. Strahm has never earned more than four saves in a season and should not be expected to take the reins in the ninth inning at any point, but those in leagues scoring holds will probably want to queue him up and perhaps jump him a round or two ahead of ADP to secure his services.

name: Reese Olson
season_outlook: Olson appeared to be on the verge of a major breakthrough early last season, in fact posting a second-best-in-baseball 1.75 ERA across 15 starts from September 2023-May 2024, before shoulder issues ultimately derailed his trajectory around midseason. He managed to return in September, most notably turning in a pair of effective ALDS appearances, and should be a mainstay in the Tigers' 2025 Opening Day rotation. Olson's combination of two strong strikeout pitches (slider, changeup) and an elite ground ball rate continues to make him a potentially high-profit fantasy starter among mixed-league late rounders.

name: Erick Fedde
season_outlook: Fedde returned stateside after winning the KBO MVP in 2023, making a total of 31 starts between the White Sox and Cardinals last season. His numbers fell off a bit after the deadline move to St. Louis, but overall it was a successful return as Fedde pitched significantly better than he had during his prior stint in MLB, posting a 3.30 ERA and 1.16 WHIP over 177.1 total innings. Fedde had a couple starts with double-digit strikeouts, but his strikeout rate settled at just 21.2 percent for the season, and without the swing-and-miss dominance, he will remain subject to batted-ball variance. The Cardinals are no longer the class of the NL Central, but it's still a decent setup for Fedde in the final year of his two-year contract.

name: Spencer Arrighetti
season_outlook: After 13 starts spanning 58 innings, Arrighetti registered a 6.36 ERA and 1.74 WHIP. His 23.8% strikeout rate was encouraging, but his 12.8% walk rate was concerning. However, something clicked at that point, and Arrighetti posted a 3.31 ERA and 1.18 WHIP over his final 87 frames. He threw more changeups in lieu of fastballs later in the season, along with improving control. Maintaining the drop will be a tall order, but Arrighetti's strikeout rate and the Astros' penchant for finding what works warrants drafting Arrighetti as a matchup play that could develop into more.

name: Michael Kopech
season_outlook: Kopech successfully made the transition back to the bullpen after a two-year run of working in the White Sox rotation. Kopech saved nine games on the South Side before being dealt to Los Angeles for Miguel Vargas, and he became a dominant piece in the Dodgers' bullpen as they went on to win it all. The addition of Tanner Scott this offseason very much changes the outlook on Kopech, since it now looks like it will be tough for him to get to double-digit saves, though he will certainly still be part of the back-end mix. Kopech, even in a non-closing capacity, should be able to help with ratios and strikeouts while vulturing wins much like Blake Treinen did last season in front of Kopech, Daniel Hudson and Evan Phillips. The lack of saves will push down Kopech's immediate value, but this would be a pricy in-season acquisition should anything happen to Scott.

name: Orion Kerkering
season_outlook: Kerkering's status as the Phillies' presumed closer of the future suffered a winter setback with the signing of Jordan Romano, but considering Romano's injuries in 2024, there might soon be ninth-inning opportunities for the youngster. Thanks to his trio of potentially elite offerings, Kerkering posted the sixth-best qualified ERA before the All-Star break (1.30) -- almost fully supported by his FIP (1.72) -- before taking a bit of a step back during the season's second half. Nevertheless, it exemplified his upside, and with Jeff Hoffman and Carlos Estevez no longer on the roster, it should lead to more high-leverage opportunities. Consider Kerkering to be one of the better breakout bets at his position.

name: Andre Pallante
season_outlook: Pressed into rotational duty with the Cardinals late last May, Pallante registered a 3.56 ERA and seven quality starts across 20 tries the rest of the way, his extreme ground ball repertoire making him a high-floor (albeit low-ceiling) fantasy starter. He'll return in the same role for the 2025 squad, where he'd probably need to improve his control in order to take a noticeable step forward. Pallante is the type of pitcher better used for streaming/matchups purposes in mixed leagues than trusted every time out, although he should be on NL-only managers' radar.

name: Porter Hodge
season_outlook: After getting the call in May, Hodge worked his way from the bottom rung of the bullpen ladder to the closer role by the end of 2024, though his path to regular save chances hit a major road black in January when the Cubs acquired Ryan Pressly from the Astros. Blessed with a fastball that averaged 95.5 mph last season along with a devastating sweeper, Hodge consistently showed closer-worthy dominance as a rookie around occasional walk issues. Relievers are notoriously volatile, but Hodge looks primed to hold down a prominent spot at the back end of the Chicago bullpen for years to come. The right-hander will still be highly sought after in leagues scoring holds and the door is open for Hodge to return to closing duties in 2025 if Pressly's downward performance trends continue.

name: Tyler Holton
season_outlook: Holton has now turned in back-to-back outstanding fantasy seasons, largely in relief. Last season, he was a dynamo for the Tigers, totaling 100 IP (including the playoffs) while serving in a multitude of different roles. While good fortune has contributed to his success -- his .203 BABIP and 81.0% strand rate in 2023-24 combined are both top-10 rates among qualified relievers -- his strides in terms of narrowing his platoon splits and boosting his control last year bodes well for his contributing third-tier fantasy relief value again. In fact, if Holton can emerge into at least a partnership of the team's ninth-inning duties, he could be quite a profitable late-round pick.

name: Aaron Civale
season_outlook: The Rays were unable to work their magic on Civale, who posted a 5.17 ERA across 27 starts for Tampa Bay after coming over from Cleveland at the 2023 deadline. The Brewers had a bit more luck after acquiring Civale in 2024, as the right-hander reintroduced the slider and pitched to a 3.53 ERA and 1.22 WHIP over 14 starts, good enough to convince Milwaukee to bring him back at $8 million for 2025. Home runs were a persistent issue following the move and Civale is lacking in terms of dominance. Indeed his Statcast page is colder than a mother-in-law's embrace, but at least the right-hander does a good job of limiting walks with a career 2.4 BB/9. While that won't be enough to sway most drafters, the AL East is a different beast entirely than his new home in the NL Central, and there will likely be more favorable matchups throughout 2025.

name: Yennier Cano
season_outlook: Cano is one of the tougher pitchers in baseball to square up with his repertoire of zig-zagging and diving pitches. The blessing of his natural movement was also a curse in 2024 in that there were times when Cano could not find the strike zone, and the walk issues prevented him from seizing the closer role even as Craig Kimbrel was doing his best to give it away. Heading into 2025, Cano appears primed to fall in the bullpen pecking order in Baltimore with the return of Felix Bautista as well as the acquisitions of Seranthony Dominguez and Andrew Kittredge in recent months. The uncertain role makes Cano unrosterable in standard fantasy formats, but he retains value in leagues where holds are a scoring category as he has 30-plus in each of the past two seasons.

name: Ben Joyce
season_outlook: A flamethrowing righty who stepped admirably into the Angels' closer role following the deadline deal of Carlos Estevez, Joyce converted all four save chances with two holds, a 2.19 ERA and 28.6% strikeout rate across his final 12 appearances before a shoulder injury prematurely ended his season in early September. The addition of a "splinker" had much to do with his breakthrough, and it's why he is one of the higher-upside picks you'll find. Unfortunately, ninth-inning duties for the Angels is likely to be handed to the recently signed Kenley Jansen. Still, if your league rewards holds, Joyce is still valuable and he'll be right there waiting to jump into the closer's role should Jansen stumble.

name: Liam Hendriks
season_outlook: Hendriks spent most of the past two years recovering from August 2023 Tommy John surgery. He attempted to return late last season but was shut down after five rehab frames. From 2019-2022, Hendriks was one of the top closers in the game but was then diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma early in 2023, and he was deemed cancer-free after a couple months of chemotherapy. Now 36 years old, Hendriks will aim to rejuvenate his career, perhaps serving as the Red Sox closer. After what he's been through, don't bet against him, though he'll have to compete with Aroldis Chapman and Justin Slaten for ninth-inning duties.

name: Kutter Crawford
season_outlook: Crawford led the Red Sox in innings and strikeouts last season, but he also led the majors in losses with 16, nine of which came during a rough second half. Recency bias is real and the swoon will be what sticks in the minds of most, though his poor finish to the season should not completely overshadow what he did in the first half when he had a 3.00 ERA and 1.04 WHIP across 20 starts. The right-hander seems to have secured his spot in Boston's starting rotation entering 2025, but the sky-high home-run rate makes him extremely volatile and difficult to trust on a start-by-start basis. Those who take the dive will likely want to deploy him judiciously, at least to start the season, until Crawford's performance dictates otherwise.

name: Kyle Harrison
season_outlook: Harrison performed admirably in his rookie season until shoulder inflammation in early September shut him down for the rest of the season. He is unlike most of the young pitchers we see today who come up and attempt to blow gas by everyone as he does not have the raw stuff to overpower anyone. The left-hander is a three-pitch guy who makes the most of his platoon advantage against fellow southpaws. The limited repertoire limits how deeply he can work into games which is why we saw him win just seven of his 24 outings. Harrison's stuff is decidedly average, and everything hinges upon his ability to locate his pitches where they need to be. Harrison would seem to lack upside, but at least he should take the ball every fifth day for San Francisco.

name: Jason Foley
season_outlook: Alex Lange was the presumptive closer for Detroit entering the 2024 season after he led the team in saves in 2023, but it was Foley who got the call to pitch the ninth inning Opening Day. Foley shut the door and went on to total 28 saves last season, tied for fifth in the American League. While Foley throws gas, including a bowling-ball sinker as his primary pitch, but it has never translated to many strikeouts. In fact, Foley's strikeout rate was just 18.4 percent last season, making him a questionable fit in the closer role long term. He proved plenty capable last season, though he had a couple tough months in May and July which seemed to put him on shaky ground for a bit. The Tigers signed Tommy Kahnle in January and still have Tyler Holton and Will Vest among others to compete with Foley for save opportunities in 2025.

name: Reid Detmers
season_outlook: It appeared that Detmers' long-awaited breakthrough was happening early in 2024, as he recorded a 3.12 ERA and 1.15 WHIP after five starts. Unfortunately, the script suddenly flipped, and he logged a 9.85 ERA and 1.87 WHIP over his next six outings. Detmers was then demoted to Triple-A Salt Lake, but he to make five starts in September and struggled with an 8.14 ERA and 1.77 WHIP. His 3.86 xFIP and 27.9% strikeout rate offer some room for optimism, but Detmers needs more consistent command and control. Still just 25 years old, there are worse speculative plays, but Detmers will have to earn an Opening Day rotation spot after the Angels fortified their staff with Yusei Kikuchi and Kyle Hendricks.

name: Frankie Montas
season_outlook: The Mets saw enough from Montas from a distance in 2024 to offer him two years and $34 million to join their rotation. Last season, Montas leaned on a mixture of his three fastballs (four-seamer, sinker, cutter) and dialed back the use of his splitter to mixed results. The four-seamer performed well as the league hit .206 against the pitch, but the cutter resulted in seven homers which is not ideal for a pitch that is designed to encourage weaker contact and not homers. Perhaps the layoff from the 2023 shoulder surgery affected his feel for the cutter. The Mets' offense should provide Montas with enough run support to win double-digit game for just the second time in his career, assuming Montas can make another 30 starts this season. Hopefully the rust is gone and his walks and homers level out.

name: Chad Green
season_outlook: Green has battled through a lot in recent years, including Tommy John surgery as well as a shoulder strain which put him on the shelf early in 2024. Despite that, he led the Blue Jays in saves last season with a career-high 17. His strikeout rate plummeted to a career-low 21.9 percent, however, after it was above 30 percent in 2023, and that number brings sustainability into question. Toronto seemed to see the writing on the wall, adding Jeff Hoffman and bringing back Yimi Garcia to effectively push Green down the depth chart. Green has carved out an impressive career -- he is entering his 10th major-league season -- and deserves credit for overcoming his recent injuries, but it was be rather surprising to see him emerge as a full-time closer suddenly at nearly 34 years old.

name: Evan Phillips
season_outlook: Phillips led the Dodgers in saves during the 2023 and 2024 regular seasons with 24 and 18, respectively, but he faces several new, daunting obstacles in Tanner Scott and Kirby Yates entering 2025. A bout of arm fatigue kept Phillips off the World Series roster, though he is expected to be ready to go for spring training. While the right-hander's numbers were closer-worthy in 2023, they were less so last season, as opponents combined to bat more than 50 points higher against Phillips. There is little doubt that he will fill a prominent spot in the Los Angeles bullpen, if healthy, and the door is not closed on him earning additional saves. It's just that the primary ninth-inning role may be out of reach at this point.
